reading.title: Rosa Parks Stays in Her Seat
reading.purpose: Read how one calm choice on a bus led to a long, peaceful effort for fairness.
paras: On December 1, 1955, Rosa Parks rode a city bus home from work in Montgomery, Alabama. A local rule said Black riders had to give up their seats when white riders needed them. The driver ordered Mrs. Parks to move. She quietly refused, and the police arrested her.

Mrs. Parks was not a rebel looking for trouble. She worked as a seamstress and belonged to the NAACP, a group that worked for equal rights. Her choice came from conviction, a strong belief that every person deserves fair treatment. She felt the bus rule was an injustice, and she was tired of giving in.
To defy a rule means to refuse openly to obey it, and she did this without raising her voice. She stayed calm and polite, and she kept her dignity even while she was being arrested.

Four days later, local leaders began a campaign to stop riding the city buses. For 381 days, thousands of people walked, shared car rides, or took taxis. They vowed to keep going until the rule changed. Their devotion to the cause held the plan together, even on long, hot walks to work.

In November 1956, the Supreme Court ruled that separating riders by race on city buses was against the Constitution, and the boycott ended. Many people called Mrs. Parks's action noble, and others called it valiant.

qs.q: In paragraph 3, to "defy" a rule means to
choices: write it down so others can read it
change it by taking a vote at a meeting
qs.why: The sentence defines it: to defy a rule "means to refuse openly to obey it."

qs.q: Which sentence shows what Mrs. Parks believed?
choices: She worked as a seamstress and belonged to the NAACP, a group that worked for equal rights.
The driver ordered Mrs. Parks to move.
Four days later, local leaders began a campaign to stop riding the city buses.
Her choice came from conviction, a strong belief that every person deserves fair treatment.
qs.why: This sentence names her belief directly: every person deserves fair treatment.

ev.text: Her choice came from conviction, a strong belief that every person deserves fair treatment.

qs.q: What does paragraph 4 suggest about the people who joined the bus campaign?
choices: They did not mind walking long distances every single day of the week.
They joined because the city offered them free taxi rides to work.
They accepted hard days because they cared about a fair rule.
They stopped going to work until the buses were changed.
qs.why: They kept walking on long, hot days for 381 days, which shows they valued fairness more than an easy trip.

qs.q: What is the main idea of this reading?
choices: Rosa Parks planned the whole campaign alone and led every walk in town.
One calm refusal helped start a long, peaceful effort for fairness.
Montgomery buses stopped running for a whole year because of a big storm.
A city rule can only be changed by the police and the mayor together.
qs.why: Her calm refusal came first, and thousands of people then joined a peaceful campaign that helped end the rule.

clues.text: to refuse openly to obey it
a strong belief that every person deserves fair treatment
to stop riding the city buses

reading.retellFrame: Rosa Parks showed ___ when she ___, and later ___.

needsReview.reason: Simplified history: 'vowed to keep going' paraphrases the 5 December 1955 mass meeting that voted to continue the boycott; 381 days and 'thousands of people' are the standard figures.
Seamstress, NAACP membership and 'tired of giving in' (a paraphrase of her own later account) are well documented; confirm tone and wording for a grade 5 reader.
The Supreme Court ruling was 13 November 1956 (Browder v. Gayle), simplified here to 'against the Constitution'.
